quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer: It may be: WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.3 requires text to have at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio, or 3:1 for large-scale text; inactive, decorative, non-visible text and text in certain pictures, as well as logos and brand names, have no contrast requirement. [3] WCAG 2.2 Level AAA, Success Criterion 1.4.6 requires 7:1, or 4.5:1 for large-scale text, with the same listed exceptions. [2]

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer: For WCAG 2.2 Level AA, SC 2.5.8 requires pointer targets to be at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, unless an exception applies; spacing between undersized targets may qualify as an exception.[2] For Level AAA, SC 2.5.5 requires targets to be at least 44 × 44 CSS pixels, with its stated exceptions.[1]

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer: For text, WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.3 requires large text to have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. [1] For icons, Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.11 requires visual information needed to identify a user interface component or state to have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors, with exceptions for inactive components and components whose appearance the author has not modified. [3]

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) is Level AA, while SC 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) is Level AAA. [1][2] Technique G18 describes a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 and applies to both criteria, but the sources do not state the specific contrast thresholds or other differences between the criteria. [2]

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer: WCAG 2.2 Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast, does not require inactive user interface components, such as disabled controls, to meet contrast requirements. [1][3][4]

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer: The sources do not state whether logos are exempt from contrast requirements, so I don't know. [1][2]

quality.question: Which success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2?
quality.answer:
The new WCAG 2.2 success criteria are: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA), 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (AAA), and 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) [2].
They also include 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA), 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A), and 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A) [2].
The remaining new criteria are 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA) and 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (AAA) [2].

quality.question: Is 4.1.1 Parsing still required?
quality.answer: No. WCAG 2.2 removed Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing, so it is not a WCAG 2.2 requirement.[1][5] Authors required by policy to conform to WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 may still need to test and report it.[5]

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: For WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.10 requires vertically scrolling content to be presented at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels without two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that requires a two-dimensional layout. [5]

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer: At Level AA, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1 allows content to flash no more than three times in any one-second period; flashing more often is allowed only if it is below the general flash and red flash thresholds. [1]

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer: Yes, but WCAG 2.2 Level A, Success Criterion 1.1.1 requires text alternatives that identify and describe the CAPTCHA’s purpose, and alternative CAPTCHA forms using different sensory output modes to accommodate different disabilities. [2]

quality.question: minimun constrast for txt
quality.answer: WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.3, requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text and images of text. Large-scale text requires at least 3:1; exceptions include inactive interface components, decorative or invisible text, certain text within images, and logos, which have no contrast requirement. [2]
